title: Reframing Success
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino argues that success defined as students completing a task or getting full marks in a single lesson is a shallow proxy for real learning, which requires retrieval and application weeks or months later. Drawing on Robert Bjork's concept of desirable difficulties and Paul Kirschner's definition of learning as a change in long-term memory, she argues students still need early wins to build the belief that they are capable, but those wins should not come at the expense of productive struggle. She uses Efrat Furst's memory pyramid (attention, encoding, consolidation, retrieval) and self-determination theory's three needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) to explain why easy, effortless success can actually undermine motivation. Contrasting simple recall questions with harder application and prediction questions on the same biology content, she shows how question design itself can either reinforce or undercut a surface-level view of success.
points: Castelino's central move is separating in-the-moment performance from durable learning, citing Paul Kirschner's definition that learning is a change in long-term memory, not a correct answer in the room.
She applies Robert Bjork's desirable difficulties to argue that easy, error-free success is quickly forgotten, so early wins need to coexist with productive struggle rather than replace it.

Her self-determination theory argument is counterintuitive: a student who always scores 100% without effort doesn't actually experience competence, because they've never had to overcome anything to get there.
The worked biology example -- contrasting definition-recall questions with prediction and application questions on the same content -- makes the abstract argument concrete and classroom-usable.
quotes: When students achieve full marks without effort, or when they sail through an activity without really thinking, the success is shallow.
As Paul Kirschner says, learning is a change in long-term memory.

Robert Bjork’s concept of desirable difficulties is helpful here. When students are asked to engage in effortful retrieval, when they grapple with concepts and experience some struggle, the learning becomes more durable.
A student who always gets one hundred percent without effort does not truly experience competence, because they have not had to struggle and overcome anything.
I have made the mistake of relying on these surface-level questions to prepare my students for assessments when the goal should be on long-term learning.
We show them that success is not about perfection today, but about growth tomorrow.
